title: The forgiveness project
hookLine: Fred Luskin's Stanford work taught people to change the story they tell about a hurt

cards: A grievance often comes with a script.

Somebody at dinner asks what happened with the old roommate, or a boss from a job long gone, and the story rolls out the same way it did last time: the same villain, the same turning point, the same ending, word for word, like a song on repeat.
Fred Luskin, a psychologist at Stanford, gave that script a name: the grievance story.
In the Stanford Forgiveness Project he taught people to notice how they tell their stories, and then to try telling them a different way.

teach.b: Luskin reports in his book Forgive for Good that people who went through his forgiveness training came out with less hurt and less anger than before. Not none. Less.
That's the modest, honest claim, and it's the one to keep. In Luskin's account, a story told often enough becomes a groove. Each retelling walks the same path and wears it a little deeper.
He also points to what he calls unenforceable rules: things we expect from other people that we have no power to make them do. Be fair to me. Never lie to me.
Remember my birthday. Good hopes, all of them. But when a rule can't be enforced, the hurt keeps going off every time it's broken, like an alarm nobody can reach.

An old voice says something close. Epictetus, the Stoic teacher, put it this way in George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things."
The thing that happened stays what it was. What can move is the opinion laid over it.

teach.h: THE SAME FACTS, A NEW CENTER.
teach.b: So Luskin invites people to retell the same story with themselves cast differently: not only as the one it happened to, but as the one who came through it and is still learning.
The facts don't change. The villain is still in the story. What changes is where the story ends, and who's at the center when it does.

how: In forgiveness workshops based on Fred Luskin's approach, people write or speak their grievance story, look at the rules they expected others to follow, and practice telling the story again with themselves as the one who came through it.

games.q: a friend expects people to always be fair to her, and she's hurt every time someone isn't. what would Luskin call her expectation?
games.why: an unenforceable rule: a good hope that she has no power to make anyone keep, so it keeps going off like an alarm.

practice: Bring up one grievance you've told more than once, and retell it kindly in three plain sentences: what happened, what it cost, and what you've done since and know now.
Keep the other person in it, no nicer than they were; just let the last sentence be about you moving, and say it once more, slowly.

orig.note: Greek, from Epictetus, Enchiridion 5: the opinions or judgments people hold about things. Long translates it "opinions".
